title: The Nirmalas
hookLine: scholars who, tradition says, were sent to study Sanskrit learning in Benares

lines: A ROAD EAST, TO THE GANGES.
WHY WOULD A GURU SEND THEM?
cards: Why would a Guru send his Sikhs away to study under teachers of another tradition? Follow the road east, toward the holy city on the Ganges.
A few young Sikhs walk it with bundles on their backs, heading for teachers who may never have taught a Sikh before.
They'll sit on the floor with students of another tradition, learn a difficult old language, memorize grammar until their heads ache, and read books in a script that's new to them.
Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh sent them. The order that traces itself to those students is today's word.

teach.h: TRADITION: SENT TO BENARES TO STUDY.
teach.b: The story first, as tradition tells it.

Guru Gobind Singh wanted Sikhs who could read the learning of the classical Indian schools for themselves: Sanskrit grammar, philosophy, the old texts learned men of his day quoted in their arguments.
So, tradition says, he sent a small band of Sikhs to Benares, the city on the Ganges known for that learning. They came back as scholars, and the Nirmalas trace their order to them.
Some accounts add names, a disguise, a teacher who at first refused them; the accounts differ, so today keeps only the shape. Next, the name. Nirmal is a word the Gurus use in their hymns.
It means spotless, without stain, and they say it of the Name, of the mind made clear, of God. An order of scholars called itself by that word: the pure ones. Then, what learning is for.
Guru Nanak has a short line in Raag Asa that the Nirmalas could have carried as a motto.

In paraphrase: when learning is reflected upon, it becomes a kindness to others. Not learning to win arguments or to stand above people; learning thought through until it can help someone. Last, what they became.
Nirmalas are remembered as teachers and preachers who explained the Gurus' hymns, drawing on the language of the scholars of their day.

teach.h: A BRIDGE, AND A FAIR QUESTION.
teach.b: Some Sikhs value that bridge; some ask how much the borrowed language shaped the reading.
Both questions are fair, and tomorrow looks at the explaining itself. A Guru who thought study was worth a long walk, and an order named for a spotless one.

how: Nirmala scholars, who trace their order to students Guru Gobind Singh sent to Benares, teach and explain Gurbani; their deras still train students in reading and exposition.

games.q: you're one of the students sent to Benares. the teachers there may never have taught a Sikh. what do you do?
o: sit, learn the hard language, and bring the learning back.
argue with the teachers until they give up.
games.why: tradition says the students studied and came back as scholars; the Nirmalas trace their order to them.

practice: Choose something hard you've been avoiding, a page you skipped, a passage of scripture you never understood, and simply sit in front of it, the way a student sits before a teacher. Breathe in: I don't know this yet.
